applicable_rules.condition: pre-fix sees symptoms only; post-fix sees the actual code change
applicable_rules.explanation: Pre-fix classification is based on observable symptoms (stack traces, failing tests, error messages) which often surface the effect rather than the root cause.  Post-fix classification has access to the diff showing exactly what changed, revealing the true nature of the fix.  Different evidence bases legitimately produce different classifications.

applicable_rules.condition: ODC boundary ambiguity between similar types
applicable_rules.explanation: The ODC taxonomy has known boundary ambiguity zones, especially between Algorithm/Method ↔ Checking, and Assignment/Initialization ↔ Algorithm/Method.  Human agreement on ODC type depends heavily on how much evidence the rater has: Henningsson & Wohlin (2004) measured mean pairwise kappa of 0.16 when 8 raters worked from written fault descriptions alone, and their most-confused pair was Assignment ↔ Algorithm.  Where raters had the code and the change, agreement is far higher.  That evidence dependence is the same effect this pre-fix vs post-fix comparison measures.
applicable_rules.literature: Henningsson & Wohlin (2004) — kappa 0.16 from descriptions only; El Emam & Wieczorek (1998) — repeatable with code available

applicable_rules.condition: multi-fault versions contain overlapping defects
applicable_rules.explanation: Defects4J versions typically contain ~9.2 co-existing faults (Callaghan 2024).  When the LLM sees only symptoms, it may describe a different facet of the bug cluster than when it sees the specific fix diff for one fault.  Both classifications can be valid perspectives on a multi-faceted defect landscape.
applicable_rules.literature: Callaghan (2024) — Mining Bug Repositories for Multi-Fault Programs
